summaries.example: Imagine saying, “Every cat is an animal. Luna is a cat. So, Luna is an animal.” The last sentence follows from the first two. Medieval logicians studied why some steps like this must work. They also asked whether the connection must be more than truth-preserving—for example, whether the first statements must somehow explain or contain the last one.
summaries.summary: Medieval theories of consequence are studies of how statements and arguments connect. Thinkers asked questions such as: When does one sentence follow from another? What makes an inference valid? Some focused on truth-preservation, while others also looked for a relevant, causal, or explanatory connection. Earlier ideas came from Aristotle, ancient commentators, and Boethius. Abelard developed an especially sophisticated account in the 12th century. In the 14th century, writers began producing works devoted especially to consequence. They disagreed about the difference between formal and material consequences, but their work became an important background for modern logic.
key_ideas: Medieval thinkers studied how sentences and arguments are connected.
They asked when one statement must follow from another.
Some thinkers wanted only truth-preservation; others also wanted relevance, explanation, or containment.
The subject became a separate area of study especially in the 14th century.
These discussions helped prepare the way for later modern logic.
summaries.why_it_matters: These theories show that people in the Middle Ages were doing careful, systematic work in logic. They did not simply repeat ancient ideas: Latin medieval authors developed consequence as its own topic. Their questions about truth, form, relevance, and meaning still help us think about what makes reasoning reliable.

important_terms.definition: A connection between statements where one statement follows from another in a way that cannot go wrong.
A statement or step that is supported by another statement or group of statements.
When true starting statements cannot lead to a false ending statement.
The idea that the conclusion is already included or understood in the starting statements.

questions_to_think_about: Is an argument good whenever true starting statements guarantee a true conclusion?
Should a conclusion have a meaningful connection to its starting statements?
How is a sentence different from an argument?
Why might people study old ideas to understand modern logic?

summaries.example: Consider the inference: “Socrates is a man; therefore, Socrates is an animal.” It is truth-preserving if being a man entails being an animal, but it is not formal in Buridan’s substitutional sense: replacing “Socrates,” “man,” and “animal” with arbitrary terms would not preserve validity. By contrast, a schema such as “Every A is B; Socrates is an A; therefore Socrates is a B” remains valid across suitable substitutions. Medieval authors used such cases to separate formal from material consequence, although they grounded validity in different ways.
summaries.summary: Latin medieval theories of consequence systematically examined when one sentence follows from another and what makes an inference valid. Their background included Aristotle’s syllogistic and Topics, ancient commentary on form and matter, and Boethius’s work on hypothetical syllogisms and topical principles. Abelard’s 12th-century theory combined necessary succession with a stronger relevance or containment requirement, while distinguishing perfect from imperfect inferences. In the 13th century, discussions remained dispersed and often metaphysical. Dedicated treatises emerged in the 14th century. Ockham used intrinsic and extrinsic middles; Buridan defined formal consequence through substitution while treating necessary truth-preservation as the basis of all consequence; British writers commonly interpreted formal validity through epistemic or semantic containment. These competing accounts illuminate both medieval logic and the development of modern ideas of logical form.
key_ideas: Medieval theories of consequence concern conditionals, inferences, and relations among propositions, even when authors did not sharply separate those notions.
Necessary truth-preservation was widely treated as necessary for valid consequence, but many authors demanded more, such as containment or causal relevance.
The distinction between formal and material consequence developed differently in different traditions.
Buridan defined formal consequence through preservation under substitution, while British authors commonly emphasized the conclusion’s being understood in the antecedent.
The 14th century saw the appearance of dedicated treatises on consequence, drawing on several earlier traditions rather than one single source.
Medieval analyses of consequence helped form the historical background of modern logic.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic matters historically because it marks a major Latin medieval contribution rather than merely a transmission of Greek logic. It matters conceptually because modern debates about logical consequence still involve the same broad pressures: preservation of truth, invariance under form, and some notion of relevance or connection. The medieval disagreements also warn us not to assume that technical terms such as “formal” have always had one fixed meaning.

important_terms.definition: A relation in which it is impossible for the antecedent to be true while the consequent is false.
A criterion according to which consequence remains valid when suitable non-logical terms are replaced by others; it is associated with formality.
The statement or premise from which another statement is said to follow.
The statement that follows, or is claimed to follow, from an antecedent.
A consequence valid across substitutions that preserve its relevant logical form; Buridan contrasts it with material consequence.
A valid consequence that does not satisfy the relevant substitution criterion; medieval authors defined this category in different ways.
The idea that a conclusion is contained in, understood through, or connected with the premises, sometimes metaphysically, semantically, or epistemically.
A medieval framework applying the distinction between form and matter to arguments and logical expressions.

questions_to_think_about: Is necessary truth-preservation enough for logical consequence, or should relevance also be required?
Why might the same argument count as formal for one medieval author but material for another?
How does a conditional sentence differ from the relation of consequence between two propositions?
What does the history of these theories suggest about the relationship between logic and language?
Can studying older definitions clarify what modern logicians mean by consequence?

summaries.example: Suppose someone says, “A robin is a bird, so a robin is an animal.” This seems like a good inference because the conclusion follows from what “bird” means. But compare a pattern such as “Every A is B; every B is C; therefore every A is C.” This second pattern keeps working when the letters are replaced with many different terms. Medieval logicians could call the first kind material and the second kind formal, though different writers used these labels differently. They also asked whether the conclusion was merely guaranteed to be true or was already contained in what came before.
summaries.summary: Medieval theories of consequence examine the logical relationship between statements, especially the question of when a conclusion follows from premises. Their roots include Aristotle’s studies of syllogisms and argumentative topics, ancient commentators’ discussions of form and matter, and Boethius’s Latin logical works. Abelard later developed a sophisticated account that combined necessary succession with a tighter connection between the meanings of antecedent and consequent. Thirteenth-century thinkers often understood consequence through metaphysical or causal connections. During the fourteenth century, dedicated treatises appeared. Writers then disagreed about formal and material consequence: some emphasized general patterns preserved through substitution, while others emphasized the conclusion’s being contained in or understood from the antecedent. The entry presents these theories as an important stage in the history leading toward modern logic.
key_ideas: Medieval authors investigated both the meaning of conditionals and the validity of arguments.
They generally accepted that a valid consequence must preserve truth necessarily, but many also required a stronger connection between premise and conclusion.
The idea of form led to tests involving substitution of terms.
The idea of containment could be interpreted metaphysically, semantically, or in terms of what a thinker understands from the premises.
Before the 14th century, these discussions appeared in works on topics, hypothetical syllogisms, sentences, and other logical subjects.
In the 14th century, consequence became an autonomous subject, with different approaches associated with writers such as Ockham, Buridan, and British logicians.
summaries.why_it_matters: The subject matters because it shows how medieval philosophers developed new logical questions from ancient materials. It also helps explain why modern logic focuses on ideas such as validity, logical form, and necessary truth-preservation. Looking at older theories reveals that these concepts were shaped through long debates, and that “good reasoning” can involve more than one kind of connection between premises and conclusions.

important_terms.definition: A reasoning link in which one statement follows from another, or from several others.
Reasoning that moves from premises to a conclusion.
The condition that the premises cannot be true while the conclusion is false.
The idea that a valid pattern stays valid when suitable ordinary terms are replaced.
A consequence that depends on the structure or form of an argument; medieval accounts of this differed.
A consequence that may depend on the meanings or subject matter of its terms rather than only on a general form.
The view that the conclusion is included in, understood through, or meaningfully connected with the premises.
A type of statement involving a condition, often expressed as “if ... then ...”.

questions_to_think_about: Why might truth-preservation and relevance point to different standards for a good inference?
What is gained by testing an argument through substitutions?
Could a conclusion follow necessarily without being obviously relevant to the premises?
Why might a historical study examine several traditions instead of looking for one inventor?
How do modern arguments about logical form resemble these medieval questions?
